newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Americas free trade zone faces uphill slog.
newsitem.headline: Americas free trade zone faces uphill slog.

text.p: The dream of a free trade zone of nearly one billion consumers from the snows of Alaska to the windswept plains of Patagonia has run up against hard reality.

With a month to go before the next ministerial summit on setting up a Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA), the project must overcome a wrestling match for regional influence between Brazil and the United States, diplomats said.
It must also decide how to react to a courtship by France, wafting the alluring scent of closer economic ties with the European Union under Latin America's nose.

Crunch time, diplomats and trade experts say, began Monday evening in Rio de Janeiro when officials from 34 countries in the Americas started final preparatory talks for the May 15-16 ministerial meeting in the Brazilian city of Belo Horizonte.
"Rio is critical. Rio will set the tone for Belo Horizonte," said Sandra Maria Polonia Rios, head of the foreign trade department at Brazil's National Industry Confederation (CNI).
Leaders from across the Americas, excluding Cuba, agreed at the Miami summit in 1994 to set up a free trade zone by the year 2005 that would rival the European Union in economic clout.

Ideally, the next big pow wow in Belo Horizonte will produce a Ministerial Declaration stating "how and when" formal free trade talks will begin and what the structure of negotiations should be, even if some clauses are left "within brackets".
With gaping differences remaining, however, principally between the United States and Brazil, the Rio preparatory talks have had to be stretched from the usual three days to four.
Hampering the process is a tustle between Washington and Brazil, which is also speaking for its Mercosur trade bloc partners Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.

Jose Alfredo Graca Lima, head of the Brazilian Foreign Ministry's economics department, said Brasilia would like to start off negotiations with "business facilitation", basically the eradication of non-tariff barriers such as bureaucracy.
Talks on actual tariff reductions should be left to the last of three stages and only take place after the year 2003.
"It's a natural process. It's more palatable and easier for everyone," Graca Lima said in a recent telephone interview from Geneva.
In particular, Brazil does not want to rush ahead of agreements struck under the Uruguay Round of trade talks.
Washington is keen to start talking "market access", or tariffs, next year, a demand that grates on Brazilian ears.

Western diplomats and trade observers say Brazil's go-slow approach, adopted by Mercosur, has a lot to do with domestic conditions, in particular a gaping trade gap which hit $5.5 billion in 1996 and is set to exceed $10 billion this year.
The result has been some bitter carping from Brasilia about U.S. restrictions on Brazilian exports, especially orange juice, which Washington says is more bark than bite.

"Privately, the Brazilians have confessed to us that the trade deficit has caused political pressure on the government to find a scapegoat and also to be seen to be doing something," said a U.S. diplomatic source, requesting anonymity.
In return, high-ranking U.S. trade officials have lashed out at what they perceive as a "lack of free trade spirit" in Latin America's largest country and have criticized Mercosur.
Though both sides say tensions are far less than Brazilian newspapers would let their readers believe, they acknowledge that the discord has soured the atmosphere for the FTAA.
To complicate matters further, the European Union has stepped into the fray.
When French President Jacques Chirac told Mercosur last month it was too big for the Americas alone and should look more across the Atlantic, he was greeted with unbridled joy.
Brazilian government circles made no secret of the fact that they saw the European overture as a bargaining chip in their negotiations with the United States.

"Brazil's trade is geographically very balanced, very diversified. It would not be healthy for a country like Brazil to...have a great dependence on trade with just one country or just one region," said Graca Lima.
Mercosur and the European Union signed in December 1995 a basic accord that sets the ground for future free trade talks. A summit of leaders is expected to take place sometime next year.

U.S. officials admit they are "slightly annoyed" at Chirac's exuberant reception, especially in Brazil, and say they hope the Latin Americans are not suffering from any illusions about expanding trade with Europe's "well-protected" market.
